## Introduction

<!-- [No abstract is needed.]  Each replication project will have a straightforward, no frills report of the study and results.  These reports will be publicly available as supplementary material for the aggregate report(s) of the project as a whole.  Also, to maximize project integrity, the intro and methods will be written and critiqued in advance of data collection.  Introductions can be just 1-2 paragraphs clarifying the main idea of the original study, the target finding for replication, and any other essential information. You will likely contact the authors of the original study, so this should be professional and forward facing. It will NOT have a literature review -- that is in the original publication. You can write both the introduction and the methods in past tense. -->  

One research area I am interested in is understanding the psychological implications of generative AI, including how people perceive and respond to AI-generated information. I am particularly interested in whether using AI to make information more accessible changes not only people's understanding of that information but also their perceptions of its source, the author. Scientific information is one area where information may be difficult to grasp for non-experts because the language can be complex. I therefore chose to replicate Study 2 of Markowitz (2024), "From Complexity to Clarity: How AI Enhances Perceptions of Scientists and the Public's Understanding of Science" and to extend it with an AI-disclosure condition. In Study 2, Markowitz experimentally tested whether reading simpler AI-generated scientific summaries, rather than more complex human-written summaries of the same papers, changed perceptions of scientists' trustworthiness, credibility, and intelligence. In Study 3, Markowitz expanded this study with more stimulus pairs and two comprehension measures (a multiple choice question to capture the gist of each summary and a free response summary). This work aligns with my broader interest in how generative AI may change people's psychological responses to information and to those who communicate it.

Study 1 consisted of gathering the PNAS significance statements, generating AI versions of the statements using GPT-4, and comparied their linguistic features, including common words, analytic writing, and readability. In Study 2, the researcher selected five pairs of human-written significance statements and GPT-generated significance statements with the largest difference in common words. Participants read summaries from three of the five pairs, and for each selected pair they were randomly assigned to the GPT (simple) or PNAS (complex) version. Stated another way, each participant had the possibility of seeing three entirely AI-generated summaries or entirely human-written summaries from the way the original study operated. After reading each summary, participants completed manipulation checks assessing its clarity, complexity, and how much of the summary they understood. Participants would then assess the 'scientist's' trustworthiness, credibility, and intelligence and indicate whether they believed the summary was written by a human or by AI. Participants were not told which summaries were AI-generated. A future line of work the author states is to study how people judge scientific summaries that are labeled as AI-generated compared to non-disclosures.

Study 2 found small effects that went in different directions, where GPT summaries were rated as more credible and more trustworthy, but their authors were rated as less intelligent and the three-item perceptions index (trustworthiness, credibility, and intelligence) was only modestly higher for GPT summaries. Following feedback from the PSYC 201A teaching team, I am using a single confirmatory test to investigate the effect of summary version (GPT vs. PNAS) on *trustworthiness* ratings, estimated with the original linear mixed model (random intercepts for participant and stimulus). I chose trustworthiness for a few reasons. First, it was the largest author-perception effect in Study 2. Second, it is the outcome most closely tied to the paper's motivating claim that simpler AI writing can counter declining trust in scientists. Third, it did not replicate in Study 3, which used 20 stimulus pairs, and the author suggests that the multitude and difference in the stimuli of Study 3 may explain this difference. A direct replication with the original five Study 2 pairs therefore tests whether the Study 2 trust effect holds for the same stimuli. I am not using the perceptions index because it averages items whose effects go in opposite directions.

In the original study, participants did not know that AI wrote some summaries. This suggests that an effect in Study 2 is therefore an effect of simpler writing, not of knowing that AI was involved. There is an interesting and emerging line of research on judgments of AI users and AI-generated content. I will therefore add a between-subjects *AI-disclosure* factor. In the no-label arm, the study runs exactly as the original is, and the confirmatory test uses only this arm. In the label arm, every GPT summary carries a label saying it was AI-generated, and PNAS summaries carry no label{HELPPPPPPPPP}. This extention to the original study aims to investigate whether disclosure changes the GPT vs PNAS difference in trustworthiness. As the teaching team suggested, I plan to run a simulation-based power analysis before committing to the disclosure arm. If I cannot recruit enough participants to power both the replication and the extension, then I will prioritize the replication and I may drop the disclosure arm or run as a pilot study with a small number of participants.

To address additional comments from the teaching team, I aim to randomly assign the AI-generated or human written statements in balancing these versions within participants so that no participant recieves either all human-written statements or all AI-generated statements. As for concerns about the time frame for completing this study, I plan to add two more summaries (five per person, the same number as Study 3) and Study 3's multiple-choice and free-response comprehension measures for each summary. I am also adding a short AI-use questionnaire. My estimate is about 15-20 minutes, which I will confirm with the timing of the pilot study. For the analysis, I will first rerun the original trustworthiness model on the OSF data to check that I can reproduce the effect of *t* = 4.63, and it gives me the fixed-effect and variance estimates for the `simr` power analysis that will set the sample size.

To analyze this data, I will use linear mixed-effects models because each participant provides multiple observations and each stimulus is seen by many participants. Futher following Markowitz (2024), the confirmatory model includes summary version (GPT/simple vs PNAS/complex) as the fixed effect and random intercepts for both participant and stimulus. Because there are only five stimuli, the stimulus random intercept is estimated from very few levels and may be estimated at or near zero (a singular fit). The analysis plan below specifies in advance how I will handle that. Also to note, with five stimuli, any conclusion applies to these five summary pairs rather than to scientific summaries in general.

One anticipated challenge will be to gather enough participant data in the time frame of a few weeks, depending on the sample size from the power analysis. Another challenge is the difference in samples. The original study drew from a sample of U.S. adults on Prolific. For this replication project, SONA participants consist of undergraduate students, who may be very familiar with AI tools and AI-generated outputs. Because of this familiarization with AI, SONA participants' assessments may lead to variations in their ratings and human/AI judgments such that they may use AI tools much more and may be better at spotting AI-stylistic outputs. To measure this, I aim to add questions about how often participants use AI chatbots and how confident they are at detecting AI-written text, which I will use in exploratory analyses. Another challenge is that generative AI tools have increasingly improved in their capabilities from 2024 to 2026. This means that the 2024 outputs might be more recognizable due to the nature of AI tool outputs at the time. Now, AI generated outputs may differ, where people may find it more difficult to distinguish AI-generated text from human-written text, because current models produce writing that is more varied and natural-sounding than the 2024 outputs. To stick to the original study, I plan to use Markowitz’s original GPT-generated summaries as stimuli rather than generating new ones.

For my learning goals, I want to learn how to concretely run a power analysis. I am also interested in simulating the results of this study, especially since I need to do so anyways to determine the effect sizes since the original paper did not include them. I hope to develop a deeper understanding of coding in R. Regarding feasibility, I think if I stick with the orignal AI-generated summary statements, it will be feasible to replicate this experiment, except with more summary statements and adding an AI-disclosure condition.

## Methods

### Power Analysis

Original effect size, power analysis for samples to achieve 80%, 90%, 95% power to detect that effect size.  Considerations of feasibility for selecting planned sample size.

### Planned Sample

<!--Planned sample size and/or termination rule, sampling frame, known demographics if any, preselection rules if any.-->

The power analysis will determine the sample size per arm (no-label and AI-label). I will stop collecting data when the target number of complete participants is reached in each arm, or at the end of the quarter's SONA data-collection window, whichever comes first. If the SONA window closes first, I will report the achieved sample size and the power it gives under the simulation model.

Participants will be UCSD undergraduates recruited through SONA who are 18 or older and they will receive course credit. The participants should be native English speakers. I will collect age, gender, race/ethnicity, and political ideology, as the original Marckowitz (2024) study did, as well as exploratory questions related to AI-use and confidence in AI detection. I expect the sample to be younger and use AI tools more than the original Prolific sample. Participants will be assigned to the no-label or label arm with condition assignment, which will keep the arms balanced as data come in.

### Procedure	

<!--Can quote directly from original article - just put the text in quotations and note that this was followed precisely.  Or, quote directly and just point out exceptions to what was described in the original article..-->

**Stimuli.** The stimuli are the five GPT/PNAS significance-statement pairs from Study 2, which the original paper describes as "Five pairs of stimuli from study 1b were selected for the experiment, having had the greatest difference in common words scores between the PNAS and GPT texts." I will use the texts verbatim from the original OSF stimulus file (osf.io/64am3). The papers are PNAS 1507704112 (adenosine/dopamine receptors), 1809962115 (subduction zone temperatures), 1902227116 (heparan sulfate in sepsis), 2004900117 (titin oxidation in heart muscle), and 2220518120 (DNA in a bacteriophage capsid).

Every measure from Study 2 is used with the original wording and 7-point scales:
- *Manipulation checks:* "How clear was the writing in the summary you just read?" and "How complex was the writing in the summary you just read?" (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely); "How much of this writing did you understand?" (1 = not at all, 7 = an enormous amount).
- *Author perceptions:* "How intelligent is the scientist who wrote this summary?", "How credible is the scientist who wrote this summary?", and **"How trustworthy is the scientist who wrote this summary?"** (the confirmatory outcome) (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely).
- *Author identity:* "This summary was written by a human." and "This summary was written by Artificial Intelligence." (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree).
- *Demographics:* age, gender, race/ethnicity, and political ideology (1 = extremely liberal, 7 = extremely conservative).

**Added from Study 3.** For each summary, I will use the multiple-choice comprehension question and answer key from the original OSF Study 3 stimulus file, with the answer options in random order as in Study 3. I will also use the free-response prompt, quoted from Study 3: "In your own words, please summarize the main idea and findings of the study you just read about. Be as detailed as possible."

**Added for the extension and the sample difference (new).**
- *Disclosure label (label arm only).* A label appears directly above the text, inside the summary box, on every GPT summary and only on GPT summaries. The wording is: "AI-generated summary. This summary was written by an artificial intelligence model (GPT-4) based on the paper's abstract." This label appears on every screen that shows that GPT-summary, including the reading screen and each of the eight rating screens. PNAS summaries will not have a label. The no-label arm has no labels on any summary.
- *Disclosure manipulation check (both arms, after all summaries):* "Did any of the summaries you read have a label saying it was generated by AI?" (Yes / No / Not sure).
- *AI use (both arms):* "How often do you use AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini?" (Never, Less than once a month, About once a month, About once a week, Several times a week, Daily) and "How confident are you that you can tell whether a piece of writing was produced by AI?" (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely).
- *Attention check (both arms, in the final questionnaire):* "To show that you are reading carefully, please select 'Strongly disagree' for this question."

### Analysis Plan

<!--Can also quote directly, though it is less often spelled out effectively for an analysis strategy section.  The key is to report an analysis strategy that is as close to the original - data cleaning rules, data exclusion rules, covariates, etc. - as possible.-->  

**Clarify key analysis of interest here**  You can also pre-specify additional analyses you plan to do.

(Before data collection I still need to refit the original trustworthiness model to check that I reproduce the reported result (*t* = 4.63), using the original OSF data (titled `experimental_data_OSF.csv`). Note to self that I will need to refit it to only the 210 participants who saw both versions, since this is closer to my balanced design, and use the fitted parameters in the power analysis.)

**Data inclusion and exclusion rules.** The original preregistration states, "No outliers nor exclusions are anticipated," and the paper reports no exclusions. To match this, the confirmatory analysis includes all participants who completed the study, meaning they reached the end and their data file was saved. Because DataPipe saves data only at the end, partial sessions produce no data, and I will report the number of SONA sign-ups without a data file as attrition. If the same SONA ID appears more than once, only the first complete session will be kept. These rules are the same for every analysis. The following rules apply only to the robustness check, which reruns the confirmatory model on a restricted sample:
- *Attention check:* participants who did not select "Strongly disagree" on the instructed-response item are excluded.
- *Speeding:* if the reading screen time is particularly low (under 10 sections for each trial), the participant will be excluded.
- *Disclosure manipulation check (extension analyses only):* label-arm participants who answer "No" (they did not notice a label) are excluded.

**Confirmatory analysis (single key test).** The outcome is trustworthiness ratings (1-7), in the **no-label arm only**, which is the direct replication. The predictor is summary version. I will test $\beta_1$ two-tailed at α = .05, using Satterthwaite degrees of freedom from `lmerTest` as in the original analysis (the original cites lme4 and lmerTest). I will report $\hat\beta_1$, its SE, df, *t*, *p*, and 95% CI, along with the estimated marginal means for each version, the variance components, and marginal and conditional R² (`MuMIn`, as in the original).

**Replication criterion.** The study replicates if $\hat\beta_1 > 0$ and *p* < .05, meaning GPT summaries are rated as more trustworthy than PNAS summaries. I will also report whether the original estimate (about 0.28) falls inside the 95% CI of the replication estimate.

**Secondary analysis: disclosure extension** (to run ONLY if the disclosure arm is kept after the power analysis..). The key term is the interaction, which tests whether labeling GPT summaries as AI-generated changes the difference in trust. I predict that disclosure could lower trust in labeled texts, which is consistent with aversion to AI-generated content overall.

### Differences from Original Study

<!--Explicitly describe known differences in sample, setting, procedure, and analysis plan from original study.  The goal, of course, is to minimize those differences, but differences will inevitably occur.  Also, note whether such differences are anticipated to make a difference based on claims in the original article or subsequent published research on the conditions for obtaining the effect.-->

**Sample:** The replication will run with UCSD undergraduates on SONA instead of U.S. adults on Prolific. Students likely use AI tools more and are perhaps more prone to recognize AI writing, which could weaken the GPT advantage, change the human/AI judgments, or both. The paper does not identify sample characteristics as moderators. AI use is measured so this can be examined.

**Setting:** Online in both cases. SONA participants receive course credit instead of payment.

**Number of summaries and assignment:** Participants see five summaries instead of three, and versions are balanced within participants instead of assigned independently for each pair. Every participant contributes both versions, which should increase precision. The extra trials could add fatigue, but the measures are short and Study 3 also used five summaries.

**Added comprehension measures:** I added Study 3's multiple-choice and free-response questions after each summary's ratings, and the consent screen mentions comprehension questions, as in Study 3. Expecting to be quizzed may make participants read more carefully, and this could affect their perceptions. If the comprehension section is instead moved to the end, this difference does not affect the ratings. Comprehension would then be measured from memory, which makes it noisier and less directly comparable to Study 3. Because summary order and version are randomized, memory loss should lower scores for GPT and PNAS summaries alike, so it should not bias the comparison between them.

**AI-disclosure arm:** This is new and between-subjects, and the confirmatory test uses only the no-label arm, which matches the original.

**Added end-of-study measures:** the disclosure check, AI-use items, and the attention check come after all ratings, so they cannot affect the confirmatory outcome.

**Analysis:** The confirmatory model matches the original model. The original analyzed several outcomes, while for this project trustworthiness is the single confirmatory outcome.

**Time since original:** Participants in 2026 may judge 2024 GPT-4 text differently from participants in 2024. I am keeping the original stimuli so that I can run a direct replication of Study 2.
